name: Liam Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for coming in, Liam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, not tied to AI firms, employers, unions or any party, and what you say stays anonymous. So you're free to tell me both what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'm a middle-of-the-road sort of person, so I don't know if I'll give you anything exciting. But I'll tell you how it is.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: That's all I need. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the Brookfield development, eighty timber-frame houses for a regional builder. The wall panels come off a lorry ready-made, and we stand them up, nail them together, then put the roof trusses on. I'm the improver on the gang, meaning I'm still learning, because I only started at forty after eighteen years driving a forklift at the paper mill. I like the speed of it, you can go from a slab to a roof in a week. What wears me out is the wind, because a wall panel in the wind is like holding a sail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and that's it. I'd probably tell the lads it's like the sat nav, handy, but you still have to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. I'm not fast enough yet, I need a few more years on the gang, and this gives me those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on Brookfield and the next site, get faster, get my card upgraded. Keep the weekend jobs going, fences and decking, and maybe get a better mitre saw for them if I can find a used one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty much how I feel most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned you do some jobs at weekends. What are those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fences, sheds, decking for people round our way, mostly older people who can't do it themselves. I use the AI thing now and then to write up the quote properly and check the price of timber, because my spelling's terrible. It brings in maybe two hundred a month in the summer, nothing in winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the money work at home right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace rents a chair at a hair salon on Market Street, and her money goes up and down with the season. Mine's steady but low. We've got maybe three weeks of money if everything stopped, and the mortgage is the biggest bill by a mile.

S0.say: Fair enough, it's a useful tool and that's it. It's like the sat nav, handy, but you still have to drive.
S0.think: It suits me fine. I'm not fast enough yet and I need a few more years on the gang, and this gives me those years.
S0.do: Keeps working on the Brookfield development and the next site, aiming to get faster and upgrade his skills card. Keeps his weekend fencing and decking jobs going and looks for a used mitre saw.
S0.feel: Calm, the way he feels most days.
S0.quote: I'd probably tell the lads it's like the sat nav, handy, but you still have to drive.
S0.fieldNote: He sees time as the thing he needs most, since he came to building late and is still learning. His weekend jobs give a small second income that matters a lot in summer. He uses AI only lightly, for spelling and checking prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no point fighting it, but people need help to adjust. Some of the lads would moan, some would say it's great, and I'd be in the middle saying let's see how it actually works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm a bit worried. I've already seen the factory do half our job, because the panels come ready-made. If a machine starts standing them up as well, the gang gets smaller and I'm the newest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of the lads on site are using the new kit, I'd ask to be trained on it too. I'd use the AI more for the weekend jobs, to do my quotes and plan the materials, so I can do more of them. And I'd try to build that up as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but I'd notice it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the panels already come ready-made. How does that make you feel about the next step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The panels used to be built on site, years ago, by carpenters. Now the factory does it and we just put them up. So I can see where it's going, it's the same story, just one more step along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the weekend jobs in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build them up. If the gang gets smaller, the weekend jobs might become my main thing. Old Mrs Patel round the corner isn't going to buy a robot to fix her fence, she wants someone she can make a cup of tea for.

S1.say: There's no point fighting it, but people need help to adjust. Let's see how it actually works before we panic or cheer.
S1.think: I'm a bit worried, because the factory already does half our job with ready-made panels. If a machine starts standing them up too, the gang gets smaller and I'm the newest.
S1.do: Asks to be trained on new site kit once a couple of colleagues are using it. Uses AI more for quotes and material planning to grow his weekend fencing and decking work as a backup.
S1.feel: Uneasy, noticing the worry without losing sleep over it.
S1.quote: Old Mrs Patel round the corner isn't going to buy a robot to fix her fence, she wants someone she can make a cup of tea for.
S1.fieldNote: He has already watched factory-built panels shrink the carpenter's job, so he reads this picture as the next step of a familiar story. His instinct is to grow his weekend work for local older people as a safety net. He is pragmatic and avoids sounding either alarmed or excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government needs to slow it down or help people through it. I'm not a protest type, but even I'd say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried sick. Two years is nothing when you've got a mortgage and three weeks of savings. And if robots can do hands-on work, they can put up a fence too, eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cut back straight away, no takeaways, no new trainers for the kids, cancel the TV package. Take every weekend job I can get while people still want a person. And look for any job that's still hiring, even if it's outside building, maybe delivery or care work, while I work out the next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the wind's caught the panel and I'm hanging on, but I know I can't hold it for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change, compared with the slower picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the slower one, I'd have time to build the weekend jobs and learn the new kit. With two years, there's no time for anything to grow. You just grab what you can and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hana and Owen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're going to be careful with money for a while, and that's all. Hana would ask questions, she always does, and I'd tell her the truth, that I don't know yet. Owen would just want to know if we're still getting a dog.

S2.say: This is too fast, and the government needs to slow it down or help people through it. I'm not a protest type, but even I'd say that.
S2.think: I'm worried sick, because two years is nothing with a mortgage and three weeks of savings. If robots can do hands-on work, they can eventually put up a fence too.
S2.do: Cuts back immediately on takeaways, new trainers and the TV package. Takes every weekend job he can find and looks for any job still hiring, even outside building, such as delivery or care work.
S2.feel: Like hanging on to a wall panel caught in the wind, knowing he can't hold it for long.
S2.quote: Like the wind's caught the panel and I'm hanging on, but I know I can't hold it for long.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture removes the backup plan he relied on in the slower picture, since there's no time for his weekend work to grow. Even as a self-described middle-of-the-road person, he wants the government to step in. He was honest with his daughter that he doesn't know what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people start now. Employers should be training people, and the government should be helping those who can't afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years helps, but it's still tight. I'd have to decide quickly what to learn, and I can't afford to get it wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start putting a bit away, maybe sixty a month, and keep the weekend jobs going. Watch what others on site are doing and what jobs are coming up. Then, once I see what's working, retrain into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like knowing there's a big bill coming in the post, you just don't know exactly when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what would you do while you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every month, sixty into savings, more in summer from the weekend jobs. Grace would probably try to get a few more regular clients, and we'd skip the summer holiday to the coast. By year two, I'd want at least two months saved, which we've never had.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about changing trade in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd want to see what's actually needed first. If it's maintaining the machines, I'm not bad with engines from the forklift days. I wouldn't jump until I saw a few people make it work.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if people start now. Employers should be training people, and the government should help those who can't afford it.
S3.think: Five years helps, but it's still tight. I'd have to decide quickly what to learn, and I can't afford to get it wrong.
S3.do: Saves about 60 a month and more in summer from weekend jobs, aiming for two months of savings by year two. Watches which new roles work out, then retrains, possibly into machine maintenance using his forklift engine know-how.
S3.feel: Anxious, like waiting for a big bill to arrive without knowing exactly when.
S3.quote: If it's maintaining the machines, I'm not bad with engines from the forklift days.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him room to save for the first time and to plan a move into machine maintenance. He links that idea to his eighteen years with forklifts, turning old experience into a possible way forward. His steady streak means he still wants to see others succeed before he jumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are sensible. No need for doom, just get on with planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it feels better, but I'm not sure ten years actually helps me much. I can't afford to retrain for years without pay, so the time only helps if someone helps with the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few years, carry on at Brookfield, save a bit, watch what's happening. Middle years, retrain into whatever is clearly growing, probably something with the machines. Keep the weekend jobs going the whole time as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, a bit. Less of a rush, but the worry doesn't go away just because it's further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what would you do in the early years compared with later on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Early on I'd sit tight and watch, because things change and I don't want to waste money. By year five or six I'd want to be on a course. By the end, I'd want to be doing something the robots need people for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Grace's work goes up and down. Does it feel safer than yours in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. People still want a person doing their hair, I think, someone to chat to. So she might be the steady one in our house, which would be a surprise. I'd be glad of it.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time if people are sensible. There's no need for doom, just get on with planning.
S4.think: It feels better, but I'm not sure ten years actually helps me much. I can't afford to retrain for years without pay, so the time only helps if someone helps with the money.
S4.do: Carries on at Brookfield and saves for the first few years while watching which jobs grow. Retrains around year five or six into machine-related work and keeps his weekend jobs going throughout.
S4.feel: Still somewhat anxious, with less rush but a worry that doesn't go away.
S4.quote: So she might be the steady one in our house, which would be a surprise. I'd be glad of it.
S4.fieldNote: Unlike many, he doesn't feel the ten-year picture solves his problem, because the barrier for him is money, not time. His plan is cautious and staged, waiting and watching before committing. He sees his partner's hairdressing as possibly more secure than his own trade, and welcomes that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time for any backup to grow. What would help is being paid something while you retrain, even half a wage, and a clear list of which jobs are actually going to be there. I don't want to guess and get it wrong.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much time is enough. People think more time fixes everything, but time's no use if you can't afford to take it. Ten years with no money is just a longer wait.

headlineQuote: People think more time fixes everything, but time's no use if you can't afford to take it. Ten years with no money is just a longer wait.
portrait: Liam is a 43-year-old improver carpenter on a timber-frame housing development, who switched from eighteen years driving a forklift at a paper mill. He and his partner Grace, a hairdresser, have about three weeks of savings, and he earns a little extra from weekend fencing and decking jobs. A pragmatic, middle-of-the-road man, he is calm in the plateau, uneasy in the steady picture and alarmed by AGI in two years. Even with ten years he stays anxious, because he can't afford to retrain without pay. He waits to see what works before acting and leans on his weekend work as a backup.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there would be no time for his weekend jobs or any other backup to grow.
whatWouldHelp: Part of a wage while retraining, even half, and a clear list of which jobs will really exist.
